approachQuestion.prompt: A rule is TRUE, FALSE, ALL(children), or ANY(children), with ordered child lists. ALL is true exactly when every child is true; ANY is true exactly when at least one child is true. Return the root truth value. Empty ALL is true and empty ANY is false. Examples: ALL([TRUE,ANY([])]) returns false; ANY([FALSE,ALL([])]) returns true.
constraints: The rule is a finite read-only tree with n rule nodes, 1 ≤ n ≤ 100000, depth h ≤ 1000, and no sharing.
Node and child access are constant time. Empty child lists are legal; do not materialize rewritten rules.

options.text: Evaluate recursively using true as the initial ALL result and false as the initial ANY result. ALL stops at its first false child; ANY stops at its first true child.
options.feedback: Each operator uses its own identity and returns as soon as later children cannot change its result.

options.text: Recursively evaluate every child once without short-circuiting, combining ALL with conjunction and ANY with disjunction using their proper empty identities.
options.feedback: It computes the same result and has the same tight worst-case work and peak storage; short-circuiting can improve particular inputs.

options.text: Use false as the initial accumulator for both ALL and ANY.
options.feedback: ALL([]) must return true, and starting a conjunction at false would make every ALL false.

options.text: For every operator return its first child's truth value, or false when empty.
options.feedback: ANY([FALSE,TRUE]) is true, and empty ALL must also be true.

feedback.reason: Empty ALL is true and empty ANY is false because each reaches its final identity return.
details: Return literal truth values directly. For ALL, evaluate children in order and return false on the first false result, otherwise true. For ANY, return true on the first true result, otherwise false. A list with no children reaches the corresponding final return immediately.

Empty ALL is true and empty ANY is false because each reaches its final identity return. Short-circuit only after a decisive child; worst-case all children may still be required. Child order controls which work is skipped.

“Evaluate recursively using true as the initial ALL result and false as the initial ANY result. ALL stops at its first false child; ANY stops at its first true child.”: Each operator uses its own identity and returns as soon as later children cannot change its result.

“Recursively evaluate every child once without short-circuiting, combining ALL with conjunction and ANY with disjunction using their proper empty identities.”: It computes the same result and has the same tight worst-case work and peak storage; short-circuiting can improve particular inputs.
“Use false as the initial accumulator for both ALL and ANY.”: ALL([]) must return true, and starting a conjunction at false would make every ALL false.
“For every operator return its first child's truth value, or false when empty.”: ANY([FALSE,TRUE]) is true, and empty ALL must also be true.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze method-1 as described in the revealed method. Let n be rule node count and h rule depth. Analyze the first, short-circuiting method. Include active call frames, exclude input and output boolean. Child references are not copied. No hashing or tail-call elimination. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair among the options.

feedback.reason: Demanded nodes are visited once; worst-case demand includes the whole rule tree.
details: Short-circuiting can skip work, but a chain or an ALL containing only true results forces inspection of every node. Pending operators occupy one constant-sized frame per active level.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Nested calls remain active along a path; their storage must be counted.
“O(n²) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: Each object is processed once without rescanning or copying its descendants.
“O(h + 1) time, O(h + 1) auxiliary space”: A shallow but wide input can still require inspecting every object.
